title: Infection hazards: bacteria, viruses and amoebae
audience: Pool and spa service workers and operators responsible for disinfection at public pools in SA. Figures and warnings apply under the state standard.
learningOutcomes: Name the main bacteria, viruses and amoebae that pool disinfection is designed to control.
Explain how the nose-entry route links amoebae to diving and jumping.
Connect each infection route to the disinfection and hygiene control that addresses it.

instruction.heading: Organic matter feeds bacteria
instruction.body: Organic material in the water feeds bacteria, and it comes from people, animals and surroundings. Disinfectants destroy or inactivate the harmful bacteria. Escherichia coli signals faecal contamination. Staphylococci and streptococci point to contamination from the upper airways and skin. Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a germ that takes advantage of weak disinfection, can infect eyes, ears and skin. Mycobacterium marinum produces lumps under the skin and may spread into damp surrounds.

instruction.heading: Viruses resist chlorine better than bacteria
instruction.body: Many viruses spread from person to person through pool water, and enteroviruses withstand chlorine better than bacteria do. Adenoviruses have been tied to sore throats, pink eye and raised body temperature. Enteroviruses cover polio and coxsackie viruses, as well as hepatitis A, and they can bring on bowel infections, jaundice, nerve involvement and rashes. Effective disinfection and clean, well-managed water are the main controls.

instruction.heading: Amoebae and the nose-entry route
instruction.body: Two protozoa, Acanthamoeba and Naegleria fowleri, occur naturally in the environment. In neglected water they can trigger a deadly form of meningoencephalitis, a brain infection. Infection follows contaminated water being drawn up through the nose, a risk during dives, leaps or laps. The organisms are destroyed by keeping the disinfectant at the required level in the water. The standard notes fatal cases in SA that were linked to neglected pools. Treat any disinfection failure as a serious hazard, and never assume an amoeba risk is only a spa problem.

instruction.heading: Predisposing factors and the health effects table
instruction.body: The standard's table of health effects lists how each group of organisms causes illness and what makes infection more likely. Factors that raise risk include heavy microbial loads, long exposure, high temperatures, injury, skin lesions, weakened immunity, low disinfectant levels, aerosol spray from contaminated water, immersing the head, and swallowing water. Your job is to keep every factor you control within the standard, and to report any cluster of illness to the operator.

procedure: Confirm the disinfectant is at the required level for the pool type, using the tests in “Chlorine disinfection and the 10 mg/L closure rule”, “Bromine, BCDMH and bromamines in public pools” and “Public spa pools: temperature, replacement and cleaning”.
Look for signs that favour infection: cloudy water, slime, odours, debris, and damaged surfaces.
Make sure bathers with open wounds or illness are excluded, following the operator's policy.
Report any cluster of illness or unusual symptoms to the operator in writing.
Record the readings and the observations, and the action taken.

workedExamples.situation: A public pool with diving boards reads free chlorine at the minimum, and the operator is considering reducing the disinfection level to save chemical costs.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the level be reduced, and why?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The standard requires the disinfectant to be maintained at the required level, and reduced levels allow the organisms to survive, including the amoebae that enter through the nose during diving and jumping. Escalate the cost proposal to the operator and do not change the level.

equipmentAndPpe: Free chlorine and pH test kit
Gloves and eye protection when handling surfaces or fluids
Record sheet for observations and illness reports

commonErrors.error: Treating amoebae as only a warm-spa problem.
commonErrors.prevention: Amoebae can enter through the nose in any pool where disinfection fails, so maintain disinfection in all pools.

commonErrors.error: Relying on a clear appearance to show the water is safe.
commonErrors.prevention: Pathogens are invisible. Test and record the disinfectant level.
Disinfectant levels are set by the standard. Escalate cost pressure to the operator.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Disinfection failure can allow fatal infections, including amoebic meningoencephalitis. Treat any shortfall in disinfection as an urgent issue to escalate.
Staff hygiene and PPE for contaminated surfaces are general practice, not requirements quoted from the standard.
Figures are South Australian standard values (revised 2013). Confirm the current regulation text.

qualityStandard: Disinfectant level is recorded at each check and held at the level for the pool type.
Bathers with open wounds or illness are excluded, following the operator's policy.
Any illness cluster is reported to the operator in writing with date and detail.
documentationEvidence: Disinfection and observation record with time and action
Illness report with date, detail and recipient
summary: Disinfection controls bacteria, viruses and amoebae, which enter through the mouth, nose, eyes, skin and gut.
Amoebae can enter through the nose during diving and jumping, so disinfection failure is a serious hazard.
Never reduce disinfectant to save cost; escalate instead.

knowledgeChecks.question: How does the amoeba Naegleria fowleri typically enter the body during pool use?
options: Through a cut on the foot and the open skin on the knee and the hand
Through the nose, when water is drawn up during dives, leaps or laps
Through the eye during a dive and the eyes are left open in the water
Through breathing spa steam only and the steam is hot and humid

knowledgeChecks.question: Which group does the standard say withstands chlorine better than bacteria?
A public pool operator proposes reducing disinfection to save chemical cost. What is the correct response?
options: Agree, because the pool looks clean and the bathers have not complained
Agree, if bathers are fewer and the pool is quiet most days
Refuse to reduce the level, and escalate the cost issue to the operator
Reduce the level only at night when the pool is closed to bathers
